missing_details: Domain of the initial value (positive integers)
Definition of the iterative function f including both even and odd cases
Construction of the sequence via iteration
Quantifier specifying for each n there exists a finite number of iterations
refined_question: Let f: \{1,2,3,…\}\to\{1,2,3,…\} be defined by f(n)=\begin{cases}n/2,&\text{if }n\equiv0\pmod2,\\3n+1,&\text{if }n\equiv1\pmod2.\end{cases} For any starting value n, define the sequence a_{0}=n and a_{i+1}=f(a_{i}) for i\ge0. Does every such sequence reach 1 in finitely many steps; that is, for each positive integer n, is there an index i\ge0 such that a_{i}=1?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, the conjecture asserts that the total stopping time of every positive integer n under iteration of f is finite.
justification: The name “Collatz conjecture” does not by itself specify the domain (positive integers), the exact definition of the function f in both even and odd cases, the construction of the iterative sequence, the requirement of reaching the value 1, or the finiteness quantifier. The refined question incorporates these missing details in a self-contained manner, directly reflecting the canonical formulation from the “Statement of the problem” section of the Collatz conjecture article. The equivalent formulation is taken verbatim from the same source, which explicitly states the conjecture in terms of finite total stopping time.
